# The geometry of folding {#folding-geometry}

*What makes a crease pattern a valid manifold?*

Chapter \@ref(intro) claimed that the flat crease pattern *is* the exact
two-dimensional embedding of the folded sheet. That is a geometric claim, and
it carries three obligations. The fold map has to be an isometry. The isometry
has to hold at every intermediate fold angle, not merely at the flat and fully
folded ends. And the pattern has to fold at all — a set of lines drawn on paper
is not automatically the crease pattern of anything.

This chapter discharges the three obligations in that order, and then states
plainly the one standard assumption that the resulting object breaks.

## Developability {#geom-developable}

A surface is **developable** if every point has a neighbourhood isometric to a
subset of the plane. For a smooth surface this is equivalent to vanishing
Gaussian curvature, $K \equiv 0$, and the equivalence is the useful direction
here: Gauss's *Theorema Egregium* says $K$ is determined by the first
fundamental form alone, so it is invariant under any isometry, however violent
the ambient bending. A flat sheet has $K \equiv 0$. Anything isometric to it
does too.

A folded sheet is not smooth, so "$K \equiv 0$ everywhere" needs to be said
carefully. Split the folded surface into its three strata.

**Facets.** A facet is planar. Both principal curvatures are zero, so
$K = 0$ and $H = 0$. Nothing to argue about.

**Creases.** Along a crease the surface bends about a single line. Replace the
crease by a cylindrical fillet of radius $\varepsilon$ and the fillet is a
piece of a cylinder: one principal curvature is $1/\varepsilon$, the other is
exactly $0$ along the ruling, and the product is $0$ for every $\varepsilon$.
The intrinsic geometry never notices the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$. This is the
familiar fact that rolling paper into a tube changes no distance measured *on*
the paper. Mean curvature, by contrast, blows up: $H$ becomes a measure
concentrated on the crease.

**Vertices.** All the Gaussian curvature a piecewise-flat surface is capable of
carrying sits at its vertices, and it is not a pointwise density but an atom.
By Gauss–Bonnet applied to a small disc around a vertex $v$ with incident
sector angles $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$, the total curvature of that disc is
the **angle defect**

$$
K_v \;=\; 2\pi - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i .
$$

A cone has $K_v > 0$, a saddle-shaped vertex $K_v < 0$. An interior vertex of a
*flat sheet* has sector angles that already sum to $2\pi$, so $K_v = 0$; and
because folding is an isometry it does not touch the sector angles, so the
defect is still $0$ after folding, at every fold angle.

Put the three strata together and the folded surface has zero Gaussian
curvature in the only sense available to it: identically zero on facets,
identically zero across creases, and zero as an atom at every vertex. A simply
connected surface that is intrinsically flat and free of cone points develops
onto the plane, and the developing map is exactly the unfolding
$\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{U}$. That is the whole content of the
ground-truth claim. $\mathcal{U}$ is not recovered, estimated, or converged to;
it is read off.

Note what stays curved. Extrinsically the folded sheet is emphatically not
flat: the mean curvature is a sum of atoms on the creases, and it is precisely
that ambient structure a dimension-reduction method has to see through. The
truth is a statement about $K$; the data are a statement about $H$. The gap
between them is the benchmark.

The lattice below is the Miura-ori vertex grid, built in base R so that the
check runs without the companion package. Alternate rows are sheared along $x$
by $b / \tan\alpha$, which is what makes the vertical creases zigzag; this is
the same construction `foldbench::miura_ori()` uses.

```{r geom-lattice, eval = TRUE}
miura_grid <- function(n_rows, n_cols, a = 1, b = 1, alpha = pi / 3) {
  g <- expand.grid(row = 0:n_rows, col = 0:n_cols)
  cbind(g,
        x = g$col * a + (g$row %% 2) * b / tan(alpha),
        y = g$row * b)
}

# The sector angles at an interior vertex, anticlockwise from the x-axis.
sectors <- function(V, row, col) {
  at <- function(r, c) unlist(V[V$row == r & V$col == c, c("x", "y")])
  p  <- at(row, col)
  nb <- rbind(at(row, col - 1), at(row, col + 1),
              at(row - 1, col), at(row + 1, col))
  ang <- sort(atan2(nb[, "y"] - p["y"], nb[, "x"] - p["x"]) %% (2 * pi))
  diff(c(ang, ang[1] + 2 * pi))
}

V <- miura_grid(n_rows = 3, n_cols = 4, alpha = pi / 3)

round(sectors(V, row = 2, col = 1), 4)      # alpha, pi - alpha, pi - alpha, alpha
2 * pi - sum(sectors(V, row = 2, col = 1))  # angle defect: exactly zero
```

## Rigid folding and the isometry {#geom-rigid}

Developability is a property of the folded *state*. What the benchmark needs is
a property of the *motion*, because every result in this book is a curve over
the fold angle $\theta$ and the isometry has to survive the whole sweep.

A folding is **rigid** if the facets stay planar and undeformed throughout and
all the motion is taken up by rotation about the creases. The facets are rigid
plates; the creases are hinges. The configuration is then a vector of dihedral
fold angles $\rho_i \in (-\pi, \pi)$, one per crease, signed by convention so
that mountains and valleys take opposite signs. Not every such vector
corresponds to a folded sheet. Walking once around an interior vertex of degree
$n$ has to return you to where you started, which gives the closure condition

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{n} R_z(\alpha_i)\, R_x(\rho_i) \;=\; I_3 ,
$$

where $R_z(\alpha_i)$ turns through the sector angle between consecutive
creases and $R_x(\rho_i)$ folds through crease $i$ [@hull2020origametry]. The
solution set of this system, over all interior vertices simultaneously, is the
configuration space of the pattern. The flat state $\rho = 0$ always solves it.
A rigid folding motion is a continuous path in that variety starting from
$\rho = 0$.

The dimension of the path matters. A developable degree-4 vertex has a
one-dimensional configuration space: fix one fold angle and the other three
follow, with two branches meeting at the flat state. A Miura tessellation is
built entirely from congruent degree-4 vertices, and the closure conditions
couple them so tightly that the whole sheet retains a single degree of freedom
[@demaine2007folding]. That is why $\theta$ can be a scalar difficulty dial at
all rather than a high-dimensional configuration nobody could sweep.

Non-rigid folding is the alternative, and it is not exotic. Flat-foldability is
a property of a *state*; rigid foldability is a property of a *motion*, and the
two come apart. The square twist folds flat but has no rigid motion reaching
that state: its facets must bend on the way and spring back at the end.
Curved-crease models keep developability but give up planar facets outright.
A crumpled sheet is developable almost everywhere yet concentrates curvature at
d-cones and genuinely stretches along the ridges between them, at which point
it is no longer isometric to the flat sheet at all.

Any of these would cost us the answer key. If a facet bends, the flat pattern
is a good approximation to the correct embedding with an error nobody has
measured, which is exactly the epistemic position this book exists to escape.
Rigidity is not an aesthetic preference; it is what makes $\mathcal{U}$ exact
rather than merely plausible. A third requirement comes with it: the folded
state must be self-avoiding, or the ambient point cloud is not a sample from an
embedded surface. This is why the fold angle stops strictly short of the
flat-folded limit, $\theta \in [0, \pi/2)$, and why the hardest configurations
in Chapter \@ref(results) are approached but never reached.

The fold `foldbench` implements is the simplest map with these properties: a
rigid accordion pleat, in which bands of the sheet rotate alternately out of
plane about parallel creases. A step of $b$ across a band becomes
$b\cos\theta$ in $y$ and $b\sin\theta$ in $z$, so the map is unit-speed along
the sheet and arc length is preserved exactly. It is a genuine isometry, and it
is all the ground-truth argument needs — but it is a one-directional pleat, not
the two-directional Miura fold whose flat pattern the constructors build.
Chapter \@ref(generative) states the consequences for the generative model.

```{r geom-isometry}
library(foldbench)

p <- miura_ori(n_rows = 4, n_cols = 6)

flat <- sample_manifold(p, theta = 0,        n = 400, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
bent <- sample_manifold(p, theta = pi / 2.5, n = 400, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])

# Same seed, same points on the sheet. The flat chart does not move.
max(abs(dist(flat$truth) - dist(bent$truth)))   # 0

# Ambient distances do move, and they contract.
max(abs(dist(flat$X) - dist(bent$X)))           # large
```

The first quantity is zero by construction, not to within tolerance. The second
is the difficulty the fold creates. No geodesic estimator is needed anywhere in
that comparison: because the fold is an isometry, `dist(flat$truth)` already
*is* the matrix of exact along-surface distances, which is the property Chapter
\@ref(geodesic) exploits to grade shortest-path methods against a truth they
cannot themselves compute.

## Maekawa's theorem {#geom-maekawa}

A crease pattern is a plane graph together with an assignment of each crease to
$\mathrm{M}$ (mountain) or $\mathrm{V}$ (valley). Two classical theorems
constrain which patterns can fold flat, and both are local: they are conditions
at a single interior vertex.

**Theorem (Maekawa).** *Let $v$ be an interior vertex of a crease pattern that
folds flat, with $M$ mountain creases and $V$ valley creases meeting at $v$.
Then*
$$
|M - V| = 2 .
$$

The proof is a turning argument. Intersect the flat-folded state with a small
circle centred at $v$. The image of that circle is a closed path that runs back
and forth along a line in the plane of the fold, reversing direction at each
crease: a mountain turns the path through $+\pi$, a valley through $-\pi$. The
path closes, so the total turning is $\pm 2\pi$, and $\pi(M - V) = \pm 2\pi$
[@hull2020origametry].

Two corollaries follow immediately. The degree $M + V$ of every interior vertex
is even, since $M - V$ is even. And the faces of a flat-foldable pattern are
two-colourable: the fold reverses orientation across every crease, so
"face up" and "face down" is a proper two-colouring of the faces.

Maekawa's theorem is necessary, not sufficient. It constrains parity and
nothing else; a pattern can satisfy it at every vertex and still fold flat
nowhere.

At a Miura vertex the degree is four, so the theorem forces a three-to-one
split: three creases of one type and one of the other. The assignment that
achieves this across the whole tessellation is the one drawn in Figure
\@ref(fig:geom-crease-pattern). Each zigzag column carries a single type and
the types alternate between columns; along each horizontal fold line the type
alternates from segment to segment. Every interior vertex then meets two
creases of its column's type and exactly one of each type from the horizontal
line, giving $|M - V| = 2$ everywhere.

```{r geom-assignment, eval = TRUE}
mv_zigzag <- function(col)      ifelse(col %% 2 == 0, "M", "V")
mv_horiz  <- function(row, col) ifelse((row + col) %% 2 == 1, "M", "V")

horiz <- expand.grid(row = 0:3, col = 0:3)
horiz <- transform(horiz, row_end = row, col_end = col + 1,
                   assignment = mv_horiz(row, col))

zig <- expand.grid(row = 0:2, col = 0:4)
zig <- transform(zig, row_end = row + 1, col_end = col,
                 assignment = mv_zigzag(col))

creases <- rbind(horiz, zig)
table(creases$assignment)
```

```{r geom-crease-pattern, fig.cap = "A Miura-ori crease pattern with a flat-foldable assignment. Every interior vertex has three creases of one type and one of the other.", fig.alt = "A flat Miura-ori crease pattern of four rows by four columns. Horizontal fold lines run left to right and zigzag lines run bottom to top, meeting at degree-four interior vertices. Mountain creases are drawn as dark solid lines and valley creases as lighter dashed lines, so the two types differ in both colour and line style. At every interior vertex three of the four incident creases share a type and the fourth differs."}
library(ggplot2)

xy  <- function(row, col) V[match(paste(row, col), paste(V$row, V$col)),
                            c("x", "y")]
seg <- cbind(creases,
             xy(creases$row, creases$col),
             setNames(xy(creases$row_end, creases$col_end),
                      c("xend", "yend")))

ggplot(seg, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend,
                colour = assignment, linetype = assignment)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_book(end = 0.7, name = "Crease") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(M = "solid", V = "22"), name = "Crease") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

The theorem is worth stating as a *test*, not only as a fact, because it is
cheap to check and it catches errors. Applied to the assignment shipped in
`foldbench::miura_ori()`, which types every horizontal crease by its row index
and every zigzag crease by its column index, it fails: at each interior vertex
both horizontal creases inherit the same row and both zigzag creases the same
column, so the counts come out $2$–$2$ or $4$–$0$ and $|M - V|$ is $0$ or $4$,
never $2$. The vertex lattice is correct; the labelling of it is not
flat-foldable. Since the sampler never reads `$creases`, nothing downstream of
this book's ground-truth claim depends on the labels — but a figure drawn from
them is drawing a pattern that does not fold.

```{r geom-maekawa-package}
p  <- miura_ori(n_rows = 3, n_cols = 4)
mv <- p$creases$assignment[p$creases$from == 6 | p$creases$to == 6]
table(mv)          # 2-2 at an interior vertex: |M - V| = 0, not 2
```

## Kawasaki's theorem {#geom-kawasaki}

Maekawa constrains the labels. The companion theorem constrains the angles, and
it is the one the geometry of this book actually leans on.

**Theorem (Kawasaki).** *Let $v$ be an interior vertex of degree $2n$ with
consecutive sector angles $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{2n}$ measured around $v$.
The vertex folds flat if and only if*
$$
\alpha_1 - \alpha_2 + \alpha_3 - \cdots - \alpha_{2n} \;=\; 0 .
$$

*Equivalently, since the sector angles of an interior vertex sum to $2\pi$, the
two alternating sums are equal and each is $\pi$:*
$$
\sum_{i \ \mathrm{odd}} \alpha_i \;=\; \sum_{i \ \mathrm{even}} \alpha_i
\;=\; \pi .
$$

The proof runs on reflections. In the flat-folded image every sector is laid
down on the plane of the fold, and crossing a sector reflects the direction of
travel, so the image of crease $i+1$ sits at angle
$\beta_{i+1} = \beta_i + (-1)^{i} \alpha_i$. Going once around the vertex must
return the last crease image to the first, and that closure condition is
precisely the vanishing of the alternating sum [@hull2020origametry;
@demaine2007folding]. Odd degree is impossible, which recovers Maekawa's parity
corollary from the angles alone.

Two boundaries are worth marking. First, Kawasaki is a *local* condition.
Satisfying it at every interior vertex is necessary for a global flat folding
but not sufficient: the layers must also be stacked without the paper passing
through itself, and deciding whether a general crease pattern folds flat is
NP-hard [@bern1996complexity; @demaine2007folding]. Second, Kawasaki is about
flat-foldability, not rigid foldability. For developable degree-4 vertices the
two properties coincide and the flat-foldable vertex is exactly the rigidly
foldable one with a single degree of freedom; above degree 4 they separate, and
this book stays at degree 4 for that reason.

The Miura vertex, drawn in Figure \@ref(fig:geom-vertex), has sector angles
$(\alpha, \pi - \alpha, \pi - \alpha, \alpha)$ in cyclic order. The alternating
sums are $\alpha + (\pi - \alpha) = \pi$ and $(\pi - \alpha) + \alpha = \pi$
for *every* $\alpha \in (0, \pi/2)$, which is why the acute angle of the
parallelogram is a free parameter of the pattern rather than a constraint to be
solved for.

```{r geom-vertex, fig.cap = "One interior Miura vertex. The alternating sector sums are each $\\pi$ (Kawasaki) and the mountain-valley split is three to one (Maekawa).", fig.alt = "A single degree-four vertex at the centre of the panel with four creases radiating outward: one to the right, one to the left, and two on the right-hand side angled up and down at sixty degrees to the horizontal. Three creases are drawn as lighter dashed lines and the fourth, pointing right, as a dark solid line, so the odd crease out differs in both colour and line style. The four sectors between creases are labelled alpha, pi minus alpha, pi minus alpha and alpha going anticlockwise."}
alpha <- pi / 3
spoke <- data.frame(
  angle      = c(0, alpha, pi, -alpha),
  assignment = c("M", "V", "V", "V")
)

ggplot(spoke) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0,
                   xend = cos(angle), yend = sin(angle),
                   colour = assignment, linetype = assignment),
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", size = 3,
           x = 0.45 * cos(c(alpha / 2, (alpha + pi) / 2,
                            (pi + 2 * pi - alpha) / 2, -alpha / 2)),
           y = 0.45 * sin(c(alpha / 2, (alpha + pi) / 2,
                            (pi + 2 * pi - alpha) / 2, -alpha / 2)),
           label = c("alpha", "pi - alpha", "pi - alpha", "alpha"),
           parse = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_book(end = 0.7, name = "Crease") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(M = "solid", V = "22"), name = "Crease") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

Both theorems are now checkable on the lattice built earlier. The following
runs over every interior vertex of a $3 \times 4$ Miura pattern and reports
four things: that the angle defect vanishes, that the Kawasaki alternating sum
vanishes, that each alternating half-sum is $\pi$, and that Maekawa's count
holds under the assignment above.

```{r geom-check, eval = TRUE}
check_vertex <- function(row, col) {
  s  <- sectors(V, row, col)
  mv <- c(mv_zigzag(col), mv_zigzag(col),          # the two zigzag creases
          mv_horiz(row, col - 1), mv_horiz(row, col))  # the two horizontals
  data.frame(
    row      = row,
    col      = col,
    defect   = 2 * pi - sum(s),               # Gaussian curvature at v
    kawasaki = sum(s * c(1, -1, 1, -1)),      # alternating sum
    half_sum = sum(s[c(1, 3)]),               # should be pi
    maekawa  = sum(mv == "M") - sum(mv == "V")
  )
}

interior <- expand.grid(row = 1:2, col = 1:3)
chk <- do.call(rbind, Map(check_vertex, interior$row, interior$col))

c(zero_curvature = max(abs(chk$defect))         < 1e-12,
  kawasaki       = max(abs(chk$kawasaki))       < 1e-12,
  half_turn      = all(abs(chk$half_sum - pi)   < 1e-12),
  maekawa        = all(abs(chk$maekawa)        == 2))
```

::: {.rmdnote}
**Background — the Huzita–Hatori axioms.** Nothing in this book depends on what
follows. It is here because a reader who meets "origami" and "mathematics" in
the same sentence will expect it, and because it marks a real boundary that is
easy to confuse with the one this chapter is actually drawing.

Folding can be treated as a construction system, in the way straightedge and
compass are. Given a set of points and lines already on the paper, a single
fold is defined by an alignment condition; Humiaki Huzita catalogued six such
operations in 1989, and Koshiro Hatori later added a seventh. Jacques Justin
had listed all seven in the same year, and the list has since been shown to be
exhaustive for operations defined by a single fold. Given distinct points
$p_1, p_2$ and distinct lines $\ell_1, \ell_2$:

1. There is a unique fold through $p_1$ and $p_2$.
2. There is a unique fold placing $p_1$ onto $p_2$ (their perpendicular
   bisector).
3. There is a fold placing $\ell_1$ onto $\ell_2$ (an angle bisector; two
   solutions in general).
4. There is a unique fold through $p_1$ perpendicular to $\ell_1$.
5. There is a fold placing $p_1$ onto $\ell_1$ and passing through $p_2$ —
   a tangent from $p_2$ to the parabola with focus $p_1$ and directrix
   $\ell_1$, so zero, one or two solutions.
6. There is a fold placing $p_1$ onto $\ell_1$ *and* $p_2$ onto $\ell_2$ — a
   common tangent to two parabolas, so up to three solutions.
7. There is a fold placing $p_1$ onto $\ell_1$ and perpendicular to $\ell_2$.

Axioms 1–5 and 7 reach exactly the constructible numbers of straightedge and
compass: the field closed under square roots. Axiom 6 is the one that adds
power. Solving for a common tangent to two parabolas is solving a general
cubic, so origami trisects an arbitrary angle and doubles the cube — both
provably impossible with straightedge and compass
[@hull2020origametry; @lang2011origami].

That is a theorem about fields, not about manifolds. It concerns which points
you can *construct* by folding, whereas everything else in this chapter
concerns the geometry of a sheet that is *already* creased. The crease patterns
used here arrive in closed form from a parameterisation and are never
constructed by folding, so the axioms play no role downstream. They are worth
knowing, and worth setting aside.
:::

## Creases and the smoothness assumption {#geom-smoothness}

A piecewise-flat surface is not the object manifold-learning theory is written
about, and it is important to be exact about how the mismatch works.

The guarantees in the literature are stated for a compact $C^2$ submanifold,
usually with bounded curvature, sampled from a density bounded away from zero.
Isomap's convergence of graph shortest paths to geodesics needs curvature
bounds and a minimum separation between sheets [@tenenbaum2000isomap]. Locally
linear embedding needs each neighbourhood to be well approximated by its
tangent space, which is where its reconstruction weights come from
[@roweis2000lle]. UMAP's derivation assumes a Riemannian manifold with a
locally constant metric and a locally connected, roughly uniform sample
[@mcinnes2018umap]. Results that recover topology from a finite sample need the
manifold to have **positive reach** — a radius within which every ambient point
has a unique nearest point on the surface [@niyogi2008finding].

A folded sheet fails these in a specific and instructive way. The tangent plane
exists on the facets, which is a set of full measure, and fails only on the
creases, which is a set of measure zero. That sounds harmless and is not,
because the failure does not shrink with the neighbourhood. A $k$-nearest
neighbour ball that straddles a crease is non-linear at *every* scale: the
dihedral angle is scale-invariant, so halving the radius halves the ball but
not the kink inside it. And the reach is not merely small, it is zero. At any
crease with dihedral angle less than $\pi$ the medial axis of the surface
touches the crease itself, so no positive radius has the unique-nearest-point
property, and the entire positive-reach family of guarantees is inapplicable
rather than merely loose.

The affected fraction of the sample is easy to bound. With $n$ points on a
sheet of area $A$ and a neighbourhood radius $r \propto \sqrt{k/n}$, the
proportion of points lying within $r$ of a crease of total length $L$ is
approximately $2Lr/A \propto L\sqrt{k/n}$. It vanishes only in the limit of
fixed $k$ and $n \to \infty$, which is not where anyone works; and it grows
with $L$, so refining the tessellation at fixed $n$ makes creased neighbourhoods
more common rather than less. The fold angle $\theta$ then controls how badly
each of those neighbourhoods is bent. Every failure mode in this book is
governed by that pair of knobs.

This is realism, not a caveat. The smooth-manifold benchmark is the unusual
case. The Swiss roll is real-analytic; so is the S-curve; so is the severed
sphere. Data are not. A measurement that saturates at a detector limit, an
assay censored at a limit of quantification, a regulatory switch with a
threshold, a cell fate decision, a policy that changes regime, a price with a
floor — each of these produces a support that is locally flat and creased where
the mechanism changes, which is a crease in exactly the sense used here.
Curvature in real data is more often concentrated than spread, and the
concentration sits where the interesting mechanism is. A benchmark built
entirely from $C^\infty$ surfaces systematically flatters the methods whose
guarantees need smoothness, and gives no way to find out how much.

The claim is not that these methods are invalid. It is that a crease is where
their assumptions bite, that a crease is common, and that here — uniquely — the
size of the bite can be measured rather than argued about, because the exact
answer is available at every $\theta$. That measurement is what Chapters
\@ref(neighbor) and \@ref(evaluation) report, and it is the reason the
comparison with the Swiss roll in Chapter \@ref(comparison) is worth running at
all. It also sharpens the Chari and Pachter objection [@chari2023specious]: if a
two-dimensional embedding distorts, we would like to know whether the distortion
is intrinsic to the projection or an artefact of assuming a smoothness the data
never had.

## What the geometry buys {#geom-summary}

Three properties, each earned above. The fold is an isometry, so the flat
pattern is the exact embedding and geodesic distances need no estimator. The
fold is rigid, so that exactness holds along the whole path from flat sheet to
compressed sheet, making $\theta$ a continuous difficulty parameter rather than
a choice of dataset. And the pattern is legal — Maekawa and Kawasaki hold at
every interior vertex — so the object being sampled is a surface that genuinely
folds, not a drawing of one.

Chapter \@ref(generative) turns these into a generator: how to sample the
folded surface without biasing the density, what noise means on a manifold
whose truth is exact, and what $\theta$ does to the $k$-nearest-neighbour graph
that most of these methods are built on.
